claim: miR-142 is one of the most prevalently expressed miRNAs within the hematopoietic lineage.
source: miR-142 is one of the most prevalently expressed miRNAs within the hematopoietic lineage.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract without specific experimental data shown, but is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: miR-142 is broadly expressed in the adult hematopoietic system.
source: In this study, we show that miR-142 is broadly expressed in the adult hematopoietic system.
evidence: Supported by beta-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating expression across multiple hematopoietic cell types.

claim: miR-142 is critical for megakaryopoiesis.
source: Our data further reveal that miR-142 is critical for megakaryopoiesis.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental findings including impaired megakaryocyte maturation, polyploidization defects, and thrombocytopenia in knockout mice.

claim: Genetic ablation of miR-142 caused impaired megakaryocyte maturation.
source: Genetic ablation of miR-142 caused impaired megakaryocyte maturation, inhibition of polyploidization, abnormal proplatelet formation, and thrombocytopenia.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced MK size, altered ploidy distribution, and decreased proplatelet formation in miR-142−/− mice.

claim: Genetic ablation of miR-142 caused inhibition of polyploidization.
source: Genetic ablation of miR-142 caused impaired megakaryocyte maturation, inhibition of polyploidization, abnormal proplatelet formation, and thrombocytopenia.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 3E and 3F showing reduced ploidy in miR-142−/− MKs.

claim: Genetic ablation of miR-142 caused abnormal proplatelet formation.
source: Genetic ablation of miR-142 caused impaired megakaryocyte maturation, inhibition of polyploidization, abnormal proplatelet formation, and thrombocytopenia.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3G showing threefold reduction in proplatelet formation in miR-142−/− MKs.

claim: Genetic ablation of miR-142 caused thrombocytopenia.
source: Genetic ablation of miR-142 caused impaired megakaryocyte maturation, inhibition of polyploidization, abnormal proplatelet formation, and thrombocytopenia.
evidence: Supported by complete blood count data in Figure 1F showing ~50% decrease in platelet counts.

claim: miR-142-3p targets a network of actin cytoskeleton regulators that collectively control actin filament homeostasis.
source: Finally, we characterized a network of miR-142-3p targets which collectively control actin filament homeostasis, thereby ensuring proper execution of actin-dependent proplatelet formation.
evidence: Supported by microarray data, luciferase reporter assays, and functional rescue experiments showing multiple actin regulators are direct targets.

claim: miR-142 activity is pivotal for megakaryocyte maturation and function.
source: Our study reveals a pivotal role for miR-142 activity in megakaryocyte maturation and function, and demonstrates a critical contribution of a single miRNA in orchestrating cytoskeletal dynamics and normal hemostasis.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive phenotypic analysis of miR-142−/− mice showing defects in multiple aspects of MK development.

claim: A single miRNA can critically contribute to orchestrating cytoskeletal dynamics and normal hemostasis.
source: Our study reveals a pivotal role for miR-142 activity in megakaryocyte maturation and function, and demonstrates a critical contribution of a single miRNA in orchestrating cytoskeletal dynamics and normal hemostasis.
evidence: Supported by data showing miR-142-3p targets multiple actin regulators and rescue experiments demonstrating functional importance.

claim: miRNAs control hematopoiesis and the function of both lymphoid and myeloid progeny.
source: miRNAs control hematopoiesis and the function of both lymphoid and myeloid progeny (Chen and Lodish, 2005; Lawrie, 2007; Garzon and Croce, 2008; Navarro and Lieberman, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: miR-451 plays a role in erythropoiesis.
source: For example, in vivo studies uncovered roles for miR-451 in erythropoiesis (Patrick et al., 2010; Rasmussen et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2010), for miR-223 in granulopoiesis (Johnnidis et al., 2008), for miR-150 in the commitment of multipotent myeloerythroid progenitors (Lu et al., 2008), and for miR-155 in the mammalian immune system (Rodriguez et al., 2007; Thai et al., 2007; Mann et al., 2010; O'Connell et al., 2010, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior in vivo studies.

claim: miR-223 plays a role in granulopoiesis.
source: For example, in vivo studies uncovered roles for miR-451 in erythropoiesis (Patrick et al., 2010; Rasmussen et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2010), for miR-223 in granulopoiesis (Johnnidis et al., 2008), for miR-150 in the commitment of multipotent myeloerythroid progenitors (Lu et al., 2008), and for miR-155 in the mammalian immune system (Rodriguez et al., 2007; Thai et al., 2007; Mann et al., 2010; O'Connell et al., 2010, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior in vivo study.

claim: miR-150 plays a role in the commitment of multipotent myeloerythroid progenitors.
source: For example, in vivo studies uncovered roles for miR-451 in erythropoiesis (Patrick et al., 2010; Rasmussen et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2010), for miR-223 in granulopoiesis (Johnnidis et al., 2008), for miR-150 in the commitment of multipotent myeloerythroid progenitors (Lu et al., 2008), and for miR-155 in the mammalian immune system (Rodriguez et al., 2007; Thai et al., 2007; Mann et al., 2010; O'Connell et al., 2010, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior in vivo study.

claim: miR-155 plays a role in the mammalian immune system.
source: For example, in vivo studies uncovered roles for miR-451 in erythropoiesis (Patrick et al., 2010; Rasmussen et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2010), for miR-223 in granulopoiesis (Johnnidis et al., 2008), for miR-150 in the commitment of multipotent myeloerythroid progenitors (Lu et al., 2008), and for miR-155 in the mammalian immune system (Rodriguez et al., 2007; Thai et al., 2007; Mann et al., 2010; O'Connell et al., 2010, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior in vivo studies.

claim: Megakaryocytes display a distinctive miRNA expression pattern.
source: Megakaryocytes (MKs) display a distinctive miRNA expression pattern (Garzon et al., 2006; Opalinska et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Functional genetic studies dissecting the role of miRNA in megakaryopoiesis are still limited.
source: However, functional genetic studies dissecting the role of miRNA in megakaryopoiesis are still limited.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of publication.

claim: miR-142 is a hematopoietic-specific miRNA.
source: In the present work, we focused on miR-142, a hematopoietic-specific miRNA, which resides in a genomic locus that was previously associated with t(8;17) translocation in B-cell leukemia (Gauwerky et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation and by beta-galactosidase expression data in Figure 1C showing pan-hematopoietic expression.

claim: The miR-142 genomic locus was previously associated with t(8;17) translocation in B-cell leukemia.
source: In the present work, we focused on miR-142, a hematopoietic-specific miRNA, which resides in a genomic locus that was previously associated with t(8;17) translocation in B-cell leukemia (Gauwerky et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: miR-142 is involved in lymphocyte differentiation.
source: Pioneering experimental evidence has suggested miR-142 involvement in lymphocyte differentiation (Chen et al., 2004) and recently, miR-142 was also shown to play a role in the specification of definitive hemangioblasts (Lu et al., 2013; Nimmo et al., 2013), and in lymphoid and myeloid lineages (Gauwerky et al., 1989; Chen et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2009; Belz, 2013; Lagrange et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2013; Nimmo et al., 2013; Sonda et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: miR-142 plays a role in the specification of definitive hemangioblasts.
source: Pioneering experimental evidence has suggested miR-142 involvement in lymphocyte differentiation (Chen et al., 2004) and recently, miR-142 was also shown to play a role in the specification of definitive hemangioblasts (Lu et al., 2013; Nimmo et al., 2013), and in lymphoid and myeloid lineages (Gauwerky et al., 1989; Chen et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2009; Belz, 2013; Lagrange et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2013; Nimmo et al., 2013; Sonda et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: miR-142 is involved in the compound immune response to North American eastern equine encephalitis virus.
source: Furthermore, miR-142 is involved in the compound immune response to North American eastern equine encephalitis virus (Trobaugh et al., 2014) and our work uncovered a key role for miR-142 in the maintenance of CD4+ dendritic cells (Mildner et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: miR-142 plays a key role in the maintenance of CD4+ dendritic cells.
source: Furthermore, miR-142 is involved in the compound immune response to North American eastern equine encephalitis virus (Trobaugh et al., 2014) and our work uncovered a key role for miR-142 in the maintenance of CD4+ dendritic cells (Mildner et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' prior work.

claim: MK maturation involves DNA replication in the absence of cytoplasmic division, termed endomitosis.
source: MK maturation is an intricate process that involves DNA replication in the absence of cytoplasmic division, termed endomitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about megakaryocyte biology.

claim: Polyploid MKs exhibit distinctive cytoskeletal rearrangements that enable the biosynthesis of platelets.
source: Polyploid MKs also exhibit distinctive cytoskeletal rearrangements that enable the biosynthesis of platelets (also known as thrombocytes).
evidence: This is established knowledge about megakaryocyte biology.

claim: The elaborated actin cytoskeleton of MKs is uniquely organized to allow cytoplasmic proplatelet protrusions to bend and bifurcate into multiple tips.
source: The elaborated actin cytoskeleton of MKs is uniquely organized in a way that allows cytoplasmic proplatelet protrusions to bend and bifurcate into multiple tips, from which platelets are subsequently released to the bloodstream.
evidence: This is established knowledge about megakaryocyte biology.

claim: Dysregulation of the actin cytoskeleton impairs the generation of mature platelets.
source: Dysregulation of the actin cytoskeleton impairs the generation of mature platelets (Hartwig and Italiano, 2006; Bender et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Actin-modulating genes are crucial for MK maturation.
source: Accordingly, actin-modulating genes were shown to be crucial for MK maturation and have been implicated in the etiology of platelet-related disorders (Villa et al., 1995; Kajiwara et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Actin-modulating genes have been implicated in the etiology of platelet-related disorders.
source: Accordingly, actin-modulating genes were shown to be crucial for MK maturation and have been implicated in the etiology of platelet-related disorders (Villa et al., 1995; Kajiwara et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: miR-142-deficient mice display an array of hematological defects, including pronounced thrombocytopenia.
source: We characterize miR-142-deficient mice that display an array of hematological defects, including pronounced thrombocytopenia.
evidence: Supported by complete blood count data in Figures 1D-G.

claim: miR-142 controls multiple facets of MK differentiation including control of cell size, ploidy, and proplatelet elaboration.
source: We show that miR-142 controls multiple facets of MK differentiation including control of cell size, ploidy, and proplatelet elaboration.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 3A-G showing reduced MK size, altered ploidy, and decreased proplatelet formation.

claim: miR-142-3p controls platelet biosynthesis by orchestrating the coordinated expression of several distinct nodes in a network of actin cytoskeleton regulators.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that miR-142-3p controls platelet biosynthesis by orchestrating the coordinated expression of several distinct nodes in a network of actin cytoskeleton regulators.
evidence: Supported by microarray data, target validation, and functional rescue experiments in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: A single miRNA may broadly regulate cell function by controlling a coherent set of effectors in a given pathway.
source: Our study reveals a novel miRNA-dependent circuit that maintains cytoskeletal integrity, and suggests that a single miRNA may broadly regulate cell function by controlling a coherent set of effectors in a given pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing miR-142-3p targets multiple actin regulators.

claim: The miR-142−/− allele was created by insertion of an exogenous gene trap sequence ∼50 bp upstream of the murine pre-miR-142.
source: A miR-142−/− allele was created by insertion of an exogenous gene trap sequence ∼50 bp upstream of the murine pre-miR-142.
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the knockout mouse.

claim: The gene trap cassette disrupted normal transcription and drove the expression of a beta-galactosidase reporter gene.
source: This cassette disrupted normal transcription and drove the expression of a beta-galactosidase reporter gene (Stanford et al., 2001; Hansen et al., 2008; Osokine et al., 2008; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by schematic in Figure 1A and citations to prior gene trap methodology.

claim: The expression of both miR-142-3p and miR-142-5p was abolished in miR-142−/− circulating blood cells.
source: The expression of both miR-142-3p and miR-142-5p was abolished in miR-142−/− circulating blood cells as exemplified by quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR, Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: miR-142-3p is the guide strand from the miR-142 hairpin.
source: miR-142-3p is the guide strand from the miR-142 hairpin, whereas the sister 'passenger' miR-142-5p strand is expressed in negligible levels (Nimmo et al., 2013; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1B and citation to prior study.

claim: The sister 'passenger' miR-142-5p strand is expressed in negligible levels.
source: miR-142-3p is the guide strand from the miR-142 hairpin, whereas the sister 'passenger' miR-142-5p strand is expressed in negligible levels (Nimmo et al., 2013; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1B and citation to prior study.

claim: Genotyping the progeny of miR-142+/− intercrosses at embryonic day 14.5 revealed the predicted Mendelian distribution of miR-142+/+, miR-142+/−, and miR-142−/− embryos.
source: Genotyping the progeny of miR-142+/− intercrosses at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) revealed the predicted Mendelian distribution of miR-142+/+, miR-142+/−, and miR-142−/− embryos.
evidence: This is a statement about genotyping results from breeding experiments.

claim: Postnatal survival at 3 weeks of age of miR-142 homozygous offsprings was lower than expected (18% instead of 25%).
source: However, postnatal survival at 3 weeks of age of miR-142 homozygous offsprings was lower than expected (18% instead of 25%), demonstrating that roughly a third of miR-142−/− mice died perinatally (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by breeding data referenced in source data.

claim: Roughly a third of miR-142−/− mice died perinatally.
source: However, postnatal survival at 3 weeks of age of miR-142 homozygous offsprings was lower than expected (18% instead of 25%), demonstrating that roughly a third of miR-142−/− mice died perinatally (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is calculated from the observed vs expected survival rates.

claim: Surviving miR-142−/− mice did not display overt physical abnormalities.
source: Surviving miR-142−/− mice did not display overt physical abnormalities, were fertile, and bred normally.
evidence: This is an observational statement about the phenotype of surviving mice.

claim: Surviving miR-142−/− mice were fertile and bred normally.
source: Surviving miR-142−/− mice did not display overt physical abnormalities, were fertile, and bred normally.
evidence: This is an observational statement about breeding capacity.

claim: The miR-142 promoter drives expression in all lymphoid and myeloid lineages examined.
source: In accordance with previous reports (Lagos-Quintana et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2004; Ramkissoon et al., 2006; Merkerova et al., 2008), this study revealed pan-hematopoietic activity of the miR-142 promoter, which drove the expression of a LacZ transgene from the endogenous miR-142 locus in all lymphoid and myeloid lineages examined (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by beta-galactosidase activity data in Figure 1C and citations to prior studies.

claim: miR-142−/− animals have reduced numbers of erythrocytes relative to WT littermates.
source: To assess the impact of miR-142 loss in vivo, we performed complete blood counts that revealed reduced numbers of erythrocytes and white blood cells in miR-142−/− animals relative to WT littermates (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by complete blood count data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: miR-142−/− animals have reduced numbers of white blood cells relative to WT littermates.
source: To assess the impact of miR-142 loss in vivo, we performed complete blood counts that revealed reduced numbers of erythrocytes and white blood cells in miR-142−/− animals relative to WT littermates (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by complete blood count data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At 2 months of age, miR-142−/− mice displayed a ∼50% decrease in platelet counts relative to controls.
source: Interestingly, at 2 months of age, miR-142−/− mice displayed a striking ∼50% decrease in platelet counts and a ∼10% increase in mean platelet volume (MPV), relative to controls (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by platelet count data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At 2 months of age, miR-142−/− mice displayed a ∼10% increase in mean platelet volume relative to controls.
source: Interestingly, at 2 months of age, miR-142−/− mice displayed a striking ∼50% decrease in platelet counts and a ∼10% increase in mean platelet volume (MPV), relative to controls (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by mean platelet volume data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: miR-142−/− animals suffer from macrothrombocytopenia.
source: Thus, miR-142−/− animals suffer from macrothrombocytopenia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combination of reduced platelet counts and increased platelet size.

claim: The reduction in platelet numbers and the concordant increase in platelet size were even more pronounced when analyzed at 1 year of age.
source: The reduction in platelet numbers and the concordant increase in platelet size were even more pronounced when analyzed at 1 year of age (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 1F and 1G showing 12-month-old mice.

claim: Lethally irradiated WT mice reconstituted with miR-142−/− bone marrow cells showed platelet paucity relative to controls reconstituted with WT BM cells.
source: In addition, lethally irradiated WT mice, which were reconstituted with miR-142−/− bone marrow (BM) cells and analyzed 6 weeks following transfer, showed platelet paucity relative to controls that were reconstituted with WT BM cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow transplantation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decrease in platelet numbers in the BM transplant model was less significant compared to that demonstrated in germline miR-142-deficient mice.
source: However, the decrease in platelet numbers in this model was less significant compared to that demonstrated in germline miR-142-deficient mice (Figure 1F), plausibly due to contribution of WT cells.
evidence: This is a comparison between transplant and germline knockout data with speculation about the cause.

claim: Hematopoietic-specific miR-142 activity is required for normal platelet production.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that hematopoietic-specific miR-142 activity is required for normal platelet production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transplantation and germline knockout experiments.

claim: miR-142-3p is the functional dominant 'guide' strand in MKs.
source: First, we confirmed that miR-142-3p is the functional dominant 'guide' strand in MKs, and that both sister miR-142 species are nullified in miR-142−/− MKs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both sister miR-142 species are nullified in miR-142−/− MKs.
source: First, we confirmed that miR-142-3p is the functional dominant 'guide' strand in MKs, and that both sister miR-142 species are nullified in miR-142−/− MKs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The expression of Bzrap1 is unchanged in miR-142−/− MKs.
source: We also confirmed that the expression of Bzrap1, a regulator of synaptic transmission (Chardenot et al., 2002; Mittelstaedt and Schoch, 2007) positioned 3.5 Kb downstream of miR-142, is unchanged in miR-142−/− MKs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and citations about Bzrap1 function.

claim: The numbers of miR-142−/− bipotent MK-erythroid precursors (PreMegEs) were marginally increased relative to controls.
source: The numbers of miR-142−/− bipotent MK-erythroid precursors (PreMegEs) were marginally increased relative to controls (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2B.

claim: The unipotent MK-progenitors (MkPs) were significantly increased in miR-142−/− animals, relative to WT controls.
source: In contrast, the direct descendants of PreMegEs, namely the unipotent MK-progenitors (MkPs), which further give rise to mature MKs, were significantly increased in miR-142−/− animals, relative to WT controls (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression levels of regulatory markers of MK development remained largely unchanged in miR-142−/− PreMegEs and MkPs, relative to WT controls.
source: Intriguingly, the expression levels of regulatory markers of MK development remained largely unchanged in miR-142−/− PreMegEs and MkPs, relative to WT controls (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: miR-142 deficiency results in increased MK numbers relative to WT controls.
source: The observed expansion of MkPs in miR-142 mutants was further supported by a concordant elevation in the numbers of CD41+/CD42+ miR-142−/− MKs relative to WT controls (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2E.

claim: miR-142−/− mice displayed a ∼50% increase in the numbers of vWF-positive MKs, relative to WT littermates.
source: miR-142−/− mice displayed a ∼50% increase in the numbers of vWF-positive MKs, relative to WT littermates (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification in Figure 2F.

claim: miR-142−/− mice exhibited splenomegaly.
source: Noteworthy, miR-142−/− mice exhibited splenomegaly and a marked elevation in the number of splenic MKs, relative to control littermates, suggesting extramedullary thrombopoiesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by spleen weight data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: miR-142−/− mice exhibited a marked elevation in the number of splenic MKs, relative to control littermates.
source: Noteworthy, miR-142−/− mice exhibited splenomegaly and a marked elevation in the number of splenic MKs, relative to control littermates, suggesting extramedullary thrombopoiesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The splenomegaly and elevated splenic MK numbers suggest extramedullary thrombopoiesis in miR-142−/− mice.
source: Noteworthy, miR-142−/− mice exhibited splenomegaly and a marked elevation in the number of splenic MKs, relative to control littermates, suggesting extramedullary thrombopoiesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the splenomegaly and increased splenic MK data.

claim: Higher numbers of CFU-MK colonies were observed in miR-142−/− BMs, relative to WT controls.
source: We observed higher numbers of CFU-MK colonies of miR-142−/− BMs, relative to WT controls (Figure 2G, right panel).
evidence: Supported by CFU-MK assay data in Figure 2G.

claim: Each miR-142−/− colony typically harbored more cells than control colonies.
source: Furthermore, each miR-142−/− colony typically harbored more cells than control colonies (Figure 2G, left panel).
evidence: Supported by colony size data in Figure 2G.

claim: CD45.2+/miR-142−/− MkPs were over-represented in chimeric BMs at a ratio of ∼5:1 relative to CD45.1+/WT MkPs.
source: In contrast, CD45.2+/miR-142−/− MkPs were over-represented in chimeric BMs at a ratio of ∼5:1 relative to CD45.1+/WT MkPs (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: Supported by competitive repopulation data in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: The MkP expansion observed in miR-142−/− BM is cell-autonomous.
source: Thus, the MkP expansion observed in miR-142−/− BM is cell-autonomous.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the competitive repopulation experiment.

claim: miR-142 activity regulates the differentiation of the MK lineage in a cell-intrinsic manner.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that miR-142 activity regulates the differentiation of the MK lineage in a cell-intrinsic manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell-autonomous MkP expansion data.

claim: Increased MK numbers are usually correlated with higher platelet counts.
source: The observed elevation in miR-142−/− MK frequency was unexpected, because increased MK numbers are usually correlated with higher platelet counts (Schafer, 2004).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge with citation.

claim: The pronounced thrombocytopenia in miR-142-deficient mice may result from a block in MK maturation.
source: Thus, since the pronounced thrombocytopenia in miR-142-deficient mice was not caused due to a lack of MKs, we hypothesized that it may result from a block in MK maturation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of increased MK numbers but decreased platelets.

claim: miR-142−/− MKs showed a ∼25% reduction in sectional area, relative to WT counterparts.
source: Indeed, miR-142−/− MKs showed a ∼25% reduction in sectional area, relative to WT counterparts (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by MK size measurements in Figure 3B.

claim: FL-derived miR-142−/− MKs exhibited smaller cell size, compared to control MKs.
source: After 4 days in culture, FL-derived miR-142−/− MKs exhibited smaller cell size, compared to control MKs (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by cell size measurements in Figure 3D.

claim: Polyploidization is an important feature of MK maturity, which is associated with effective platelet production.
source: Polyploidization is an additional important feature of MK maturity, which is associated with effective platelet production (Levine et al., 1982; Mattia et al., 2002; Ravid et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CD41+ BM-derived miR-142−/− MKs exhibited reduced overall ploidy.
source: CD41+ BM-derived miR-142−/− MKs, exhibited reduced overall ploidy (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry ploidy analysis in Figure 3E.

claim: The fraction of mature (≥16N) miR-142−/− MKs was significantly diminished, relative to WT controls.
source: Furthermore, the fraction of mature (≥16N) miR-142−/− MKs was significantly diminished, relative to WT controls, whereas the percentage of low ploidy immature MK forms (≤8N) was higher in miR-142−/− BM (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by ploidy distribution data in Figure 3E.

claim: The percentage of low ploidy immature MK forms (≤8N) was higher in miR-142−/− BM.
source: Furthermore, the fraction of mature (≥16N) miR-142−/− MKs was significantly diminished, relative to WT controls, whereas the percentage of low ploidy immature MK forms (≤8N) was higher in miR-142−/− BM (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by ploidy distribution data in Figure 3E.

claim: High ploidy number (>32) was observed in only 4% of the miR-142−/− MK, relative to 12% in control MKs.
source: Similar data were gained by ex vivo differentiation of FL-derived MKs, whereby high ploidy number (>32) was observed in only 4% of the miR-142−/− MK, relative to 12% in control MKs (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by ploidy analysis of FL-derived MKs in Figure 3F.

claim: miR-142 is essential for normal endomitosis.
source: Thus, miR-142 is essential for normal endomitosis and reduced miR-142−/− platelet numbers might result from accumulation of immature, low-polyploid MKs that are poor producers of platelets (Mattia et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ploidy data with citation to support the relationship between ploidy and platelet production.

claim: Reduced miR-142−/− platelet numbers might result from accumulation of immature, low-polyploid MKs that are poor producers of platelets.
source: Thus, miR-142 is essential for normal endomitosis and reduced miR-142−/− platelet numbers might result from accumulation of immature, low-polyploid MKs that are poor producers of platelets (Mattia et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the ploidy data with citation to support the relationship.

claim: Proplatelet formation represents the final phase of MK maturation, culminating in platelet release into the bloodstream.
source: Proplatelet formation (PPF) represents the final phase of MK maturation, culminating in platelet release into the bloodstream (Machlus and Italiano, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A striking threefold reduction in miR-142−/− MKs that were extending proplatelets was observed, relative to control MKs.
source: Remarkably, we observed a striking threefold reduction in miR-142−/− MKs that were extending proplatelets, relative to control MKs (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by proplatelet formation assay data in Figure 3G.

claim: The introduction of miR-142-3p was sufficient to recapitulate WT PPF levels in cells that are genetically miR-142-deficient.
source: The introduction of miR-142-3p was sufficient to recapitulate WT PPF levels in cells that are genetically miR-142-deficient (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 3H.

claim: Overexpression of miR-142-3p mimics in WT MKs did not yield any significant increase in PPF levels.
source: Conversely, overexpression of miR-142-3p mimics in WT MKs did not yield any significant increase in PPF levels.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3H.

claim: miR-142-3p activity is essential for proper MK maturation.
source: Thus, miR-142-3p activity is essential for proper MK maturation and its loss results in defective platelet biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PPF rescue experiment.

claim: Loss of miR-142-3p results in defective platelet biogenesis.
source: Thus, miR-142-3p activity is essential for proper MK maturation and its loss results in defective platelet biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on MK maturation defects and thrombocytopenia.

claim: There might be a continuous requirement for miR-142-3p activity to maintain MK maturity.
source: Furthermore, since re-introduction of miR-142-3p into miR-142−/− differentiated MKs restored functional identity, we conclude that there might be a continuous requirement for miR-142-3p activity to maintain MK maturity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that miR-142-3p can rescue mature MKs.

claim: Dynamic rearrangement and organization of MK cytoskeletal structures is essential for normal megakaryopoiesis, endomitosis, and platelet production.
source: Dynamic rearrangement and organization of MK cytoskeletal structures is essential for normal megakaryopoiesis, endomitosis, and platelet production (Hartwig and Italiano, 2006; Lordier et al., 2008; Thon and Italiano, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: miR-142−/− MKs displayed a markedly disturbed cytoskeletal organization compared to WT counterparts.
source: This analysis revealed a markedly disturbed cytoskeletal organization in miR-142−/− MKs compared to WT counterparts (Figure 4A) and mutant cells displayed a more immature circular profile than WT counterparts (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 4A.

claim: miR-142−/− MKs displayed a more immature circular profile than WT counterparts.
source: This analysis revealed a markedly disturbed cytoskeletal organization in miR-142−/− MKs compared to WT counterparts (Figure 4A) and mutant cells displayed a more immature circular profile than WT counterparts (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by circularity measurements in Figure 4B.

claim: ImagestreamX flow cytometry revealed a lower ratio of filamentous to globular (F/G) actin in miR-142−/− CD61+ MKs than in control MKs.
source: Accordingly, ImagestreamX flow cytometery revealed a lower ratio of filamentous to globular (F/G) actin in miR-142−/− CD61+ MKs than in control MKs (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by ImagestreamX data in Figure 4D.

claim: miR-142−/− MKs are smaller in size than control MKs.
source: This analysis reaffirmed that miR-142−/− MKs are smaller in size, more circular and exhibited a more homogenous F-actin distribution than controls (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Supported by ImagestreamX cell area measurements in Figure 4E.

claim: miR-142−/− MKs are more circular than control MKs.
source: This analysis reaffirmed that miR-142−/− MKs are smaller in size, more circular and exhibited a more homogenous F-actin distribution than controls (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Supported by ImagestreamX circularity measurements in Figure 4F.

claim: miR-142−/− MKs exhibited a more homogenous F-actin distribution than controls.
source: This analysis reaffirmed that miR-142−/− MKs are smaller in size, more circular and exhibited a more homogenous F-actin distribution than controls (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Supported by ImagestreamX F-actin polarity measurements in Figure 4G.

claim: The number of miR-142−/− MKs that were able to create stress-fibers following treatment with CytoD was significantly lower, relative to control MKs.
source: The number of miR-142−/− MKs that were able to create stress-fibers following treatment with CytoD was significantly lower, relative to control MKs (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by cytochalasin D washout experiment data in Figure 4I.

claim: miR-142 is pivotal for normal actin dynamics and architecture in MKs.
source: Collectively, these data reveal that miR-142 is pivotal for normal actin dynamics and architecture in MKs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple actin cytoskeleton analyses.

claim: Roughly 800 mRNAs were significantly deregulated due to loss of miR-142 in differentiated MKs.
source: This study revealed that roughly 800 mRNAs were significantly deregulated due to loss of miR-142 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sylamer analysis uncovered a highly significant enrichment for the 7- and 8-mer seeds of miR-142-3p among genes that were up-regulated in miR-142−/− MKs.
source: Sylamer analysis (van Dongen et al., 2008) of microarray data, from WT and miR-142−/− FL-derived MKs, uncovered a highly significant enrichment for the 7- and 8-mer seeds of miR-142-3p among genes that were up-regulated in miR-142−/− MKs (Blue lines; Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Sylamer analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Enrichment for miR-142-5p seed was not evident in genes up-regulated in miR-142−/− MKs.
source: However, such enrichment was not evident for any other miRNA including the sister miRNA, miR-142-5p (Green lines; Figure 5B), further substantiating that miR-142-3p is the dominant functional miRNA from the pre-miR-142 hairpin.
evidence: Supported by Sylamer analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: miR-142-3p is the dominant functional miRNA from the pre-miR-142 hairpin.
source: However, such enrichment was not evident for any other miRNA including the sister miRNA, miR-142-5p (Green lines; Figure 5B), further substantiating that miR-142-3p is the dominant functional miRNA from the pre-miR-142 hairpin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Sylamer analysis showing only miR-142-3p seed enrichment.

claim: Forty genes were found to be commonly up-regulated in all three miR-142−/− hematopoietic cell types (MKs, CD24+ DCs, and CD24- DCs).
source: Forty genes were found to be commonly up-regulated in all three miR-142−/− hematopoietic cell types (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: The list of 40 commonly up-regulated genes is highly enriched with direct miR-142-3p putative targets (12 out of 40 genes).
source: This list is highly enriched with direct miR-142-3p putative targets (12 out of 40 genes).
evidence: This is a statement about the proportion of predicted targets in the commonly up-regulated gene list.

claim: DAVID analysis of the 40 commonly up-regulated genes uncovered a significant enrichment for actin- and cytoskeleton-related functional GO categories.
source: Subsequent DAVID analysis performed on these genes uncovered a significant enrichment for actin- and cytoskeleton-related functional GO categories (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Half of the dozen predicted miR-142-3p targets encode for pivotal actin cytoskeleton-associated proteins.
source: Indeed, half of the dozen predicted miR-142-3p targets encode for pivotal actin cytoskeleton-associated proteins, including Cofilin-2 (Cfl2), Glucocorticoid receptor DNA binding factor 1 (Grlf1), Biorientation of chromosomes in cell division 1 (Bod1), Integrin alpha V (Itgav), Twinfilin-1 (Twf1), and Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome-like (Wasl).
evidence: This is a statement about the functional annotation of predicted targets.

claim: Wasl was recently suggested as a potential target of miR-142-3p in the process of actin-mediated mycobacterial infection.
source: Intriguingly, the latter was recently suggested as a potential target of miR-142-3p in the process of actin-mediated mycobacterial infection (Bettencourt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The up-regulation of Cfl2, Wasl, Bod1, Itgav, Twf1, and Grlf1 in miR-142−/− MKs was confirmed by qPCR.
source: The up-regulation of these six miR-142-3p targets in miR-142−/− MKs, was further confirmed by qPCR (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 5D.

claim: Cfl2 expression was found to be up-regulated in miR-142−/− MkPs.
source: Among these targets, Cfl2 expression was also found to be up-regulated in miR-142−/− MkPs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Introducing miR-142-3p into differentiated MKs was sufficient to normalize the expression levels of Wasl and Cfl2 in miR-142−/− MKs.
source: Introducing of miR-142-3p into differentiated MKs, using dsRNA mimetics, was sufficient to normalize the expression levels of representative miR-142-3p targets, Wasl and Cfl2 in miR-142−/− MKs (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 5E.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed up-regulation of the protein products of Wasl and Cfl2 in miR-142−/− MKs.
source: Western blot analysis revealed up-regulation of the protein products of Wasl and Cfl2 in miR-142−/− MKs, further substantiating them as bona fide miR-142-3p targets (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: The mRNAs of Wasl, Cfl2, Grlf1, Itgav and Twf1 are directly targeted by miR-142-3p.
source: Using luciferase reporter assays, we showed that the mRNAs of Wasl, Cfl2, Grlf1, Itgav and Twf1 are directly targeted by miR-142-3p (Figure 5H–J, Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data in Figures 5H-J and supplemental figures.

claim: The expression of a compound set of actin cytoskeleton regulators is post-transcriptionally controlled by miR-142-3p.
source: Taken together, we discovered that the expression of a compound set of actin cytoskeleton regulators is post-transcriptionally controlled by miR-142-3p.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the target validation experiments.

claim: miR-142-deficient MKs displayed perturbed actin filament dynamics and diminished proplatelet formation.
source: miR-142-deficient MKs displayed perturbed actin filament dynamics and diminished proplatelet formation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The PPF defect in miR-142−/− MKs is presumably due to de-repression of several actin cytoskeleton components.
source: This is presumably due to de-repression of several actin cytoskeleton components, including Wasl, Cfl2, Twf1, Itgav or Grlf1, which are all direct miR-142-3p targets.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the target validation data.

claim: The PPF defect was clearly evident in miR-142−/− MKs transduced with shRFP.
source: The PPF defect was clearly evident in miR-142−/− MKs transduced with shRFP (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by PPF assay data in Figure 6B.

claim: miR-142−/− MKs transduced with shRNA directed against Cfl2, Wasl, or Grlf1 displayed a prominent elevation of PPF levels.
source: In contrast, miR-142−/− MKs that were transduced with shRNA directed against Cfl2, Wasl, Grlf1, displayed a prominent elevation of PPF levels, and approximated levels observed in control WT MKs transduced with shRFP (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by PPF rescue data in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of both Cfl2 and Wasl did not yield any significant increase in PPF levels in miR-142-deficient MKs.
source: Remarkably, knockdown of both Cfl2 and Wasl, which carry out opposing functions within the actin regulatory network, did not yield any significant increase in PPF levels in miR-142-deficient MKs (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by combinatorial knockdown data in Figure 6C.

claim: Concomitant Cfl2 and Grlf1 knockdown enhanced PPF in miR-142 null MKs.
source: Conversely, concomitant Cfl2 and Grlf1 knockdown, two proteins that are important for destabilizing actin polymers, enhanced PPF in miR-142 null MKs (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by combinatorial knockdown data in Figure 6C.

claim: A pool of shRNA against miR-142-3p targets was able to fully restore PPF capacity to WT levels.
source: Lastly, a pool of shRNA against miR-142-3p targets was able to fully restore PPF capacity to WT levels (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by pooled shRNA rescue data in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The expression of a set of actin cytoskeleton regulators should be tightly orchestrated by miR-142-3p in order to effectively promote platelet biogenesis.
source: These data demonstrate that the expression of a set of actin cytoskeleton regulators should be tightly orchestrated by miR-142-3p in order to effectively promote platelet biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combinatorial knockdown experiments.

claim: Hematopoietic-specific miR-142 has emerged as a critical regulator of various blood and lymphoid cell lineages.
source: Hematopoietic-specific miR-142 has emerged in recent years as a critical regulator of various blood and lymphoid cell lineages (Gauwerky et al., 1989; Chen et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2009; Belz, 2013; Lagrange et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2013; Mildner et al., 2013; Nimmo et al., 2013; Sonda et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: Deletion of the miR-142 allele results in pronounced thrombocytopenia.
source: Using a recently-established mouse model, we show that deletion of the miR-142 allele results in pronounced thrombocytopenia.
evidence: Supported by platelet count data in Figure 1F.

claim: Proper miR-142 function is essential, in a cell-intrinsic manner, for MK maturation.
source: Our in vivo studies and culture assays reveal that proper miR-142 function is essential, in a cell-intrinsic manner, for MK maturation, including control of cell size, polyploidization and proplatelet elaboration.
evidence: Supported by competitive repopulation and ex vivo culture data.

claim: MKs require sustained miR-142-3p expression.
source: Furthermore, MKs require sustained miR-142-3p expression, as re-introduction of synthetic miR-142-3p mimetics, even onto differentiated MKs, was sufficient to restore functional maturity.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment in Figure 3H.

claim: Re-introduction of synthetic miR-142-3p mimetics onto differentiated MKs was sufficient to restore functional maturity.
source: Furthermore, MKs require sustained miR-142-3p expression, as re-introduction of synthetic miR-142-3p mimetics, even onto differentiated MKs, was sufficient to restore functional maturity.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment in Figure 3H.

claim: miR-142-3p mediates the repression of an interconnected set of actin cytoskeleton regulators.
source: Mechanistically, we demonstrate that miR-142-3p mediates the repression of an interconnected set of actin cytoskeleton regulators.
evidence: Supported by target validation and functional studies in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The dysregulation of actin cytoskeleton regulators is responsible for incomplete maturation observed in miR-142-deficient MKs.
source: These collectively contribute to MK maturation and their dysregulation is responsible for incomplete maturation observed in miR-142-deficient MKs.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing knockdown of targets restores PPF.

claim: The sets of target genes predicted to be regulated by a particular miRNA often do not coalesce into coherent networks with distinct biological functions.
source: Very often, the sets of target genes that are predicted to be regulated by a particular miRNAs do not coalesce into coherent networks with distinct biological functions (Stark et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the general state of miRNA target prediction with citation.

claim: This work provides a clear example of an individual miRNA that co-regulates a network of functionally-associated targets.
source: However, our work provides a clear example of an individual miRNA that co-regulates a network of functionally-associated targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that miR-142-3p targets multiple actin regulators.

claim: The ability of a miRNA to modulate the expression of multiple targets within the same pathway simultaneously was previously suggested in other cellular contexts.
source: Indeed, the ability of a miRNA to modulate the expression of multiple targets within the same pathway simultaneously was previously suggested in other cellular contexts.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work on miRNA network regulation.

claim: The bicistronic miR-143/145 miRNA gene cluster dictates smooth-muscle cell phenotypic switching by orchestrating the expression of a cadre of cytoskeletal remodeling regulators.
source: For instance, the bicistronic miR-143/145 miRNA gene cluster dictates smooth-muscle cell phenotypic switching by orchestrating the expression of a cadre of cytoskeletal remodeling regulators (Xin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: miR-125 family members control hematopoietic stem cell pool size by targeting a cohort of proapoptotic genes.
source: Furthermore, miR-125 family members control hematopoietic stem cell pool size by targeting a cohort of proapoptotic genes (Guo et al., 2010; Ooi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A single miRNA that cumulatively targets several nodes within the same biological circuit may serve as an effective means to control cellular behavior.
source: Therefore, a single miRNA that cumulatively targets several nodes within the same biological circuit may serve as an effective means to control cellular behavior.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the examples of network regulation by miRNAs.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton participates in a wide array of cellular functions.
source: The actin cytoskeleton participates in a wide array of cellular functions, and the dynamic turnover between its F-actin and monomeric G-actin forms is regulated by a large number of actin-binding proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin biology.

claim: The dynamic turnover between F-actin and monomeric G-actin forms is regulated by a large number of actin-binding proteins.
source: The actin cytoskeleton participates in a wide array of cellular functions, and the dynamic turnover between its F-actin and monomeric G-actin forms is regulated by a large number of actin-binding proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin regulation.

claim: The set of genes targeted by miR-142-3p contains components with divergent functions.
source: Within this cytoskeletal regulatory network, the set of genes targeted by miR-142-3p contains components with divergent functions.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional diversity of miR-142-3p targets.

claim: Cfl2 and Twf1 participate in disassembly of actin filaments.
source: For example, Cfl2 and Twf1 participate in disassembly of actin filaments (Bamburg, 1999; Moseley et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on protein function.

claim: Grlf1 is a GTPase activating protein that has been implicated in disruption of the organized actin cytoskeleton.
source: Likewise, Grlf1 is a GTPase activating protein that has been implicated in disruption of the organized actin cytoskeleton (McGlade et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on protein function.

claim: Wasl promotes actin polymerization by catalyzing filament branching together with the Arp2/3 complex.
source: Wasl, on the other hand, promotes actin polymerization by catalyzing filament branching together with the Arp2/3 complex (Rotty et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on protein function.

claim: miR-142 deficiency destabilizes feedback loops required for actin filament homeostasis, stress fiber formation, and actin remodeling.
source: Thus, miR-142 deficiency destabilizes feedback loops required for actin filament homeostasis, stress fiber formation, and actin remodeling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that miR-142 targets multiple actin regulators with opposing functions.

claim: Destabilization of actin regulatory feedback loops impairs proplatelet generation.
source: This in turn impairs proplatelet generation and plausibly other MK-intrinsic cellular functions, such as endomitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion linking the actin defects to the observed phenotypes.

claim: Additional miR-142-3p targets may participate in the regulation of MK differentiation.
source: It is also likely that additional miR-142-3p targets participate in the regulation of MK differentiation.
evidence: This is speculation about other potential targets.

claim: The over-representation of miR-142-deficient MkPs might result from a dysregulation of a distinct set of targets that are not necessarily related to actin regulation.
source: For example, the over-representation of miR-142-deficient MkPs might result from a dysregulation of a distinct set of targets that are not necessarily related to actin regulation.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of MkP expansion.

claim: Repression of miR-142-3p actin-associated targets was found to be sufficient for restoring PPF levels in miR-142-deficient MKs.
source: Repression of miR-142-3p actin-associated targets was found to be sufficient for restoring PPF levels in miR-142-deficient MKs.
evidence: Supported by shRNA rescue experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Knocking down miR-142-3p targets in WT MKs did not result in significant increase in PPF capacity over WT baseline levels.
source: Interestingly, knocking down the same targets in WT MKs did not result in significant increase in PPF capacity over WT baseline levels.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There might be a certain threshold in PPF levels that cannot be crossed, even when regulation of miR-142-3p is mimicked.
source: This might be related to a certain threshold in PPF levels that cannot be crossed, even when regulation of miR-142-3p is mimicked.
evidence: This is speculation about why knockdown in WT cells doesn't increase PPF further.

claim: miR-142 plays a cardinal role in maturation of MKs.
source: In summary, our analysis suggests a cardinal role for miR-142 in maturation of MKs, and in particular in controlling a network of chief actin regulators to facilitate MK terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from all the experimental data.

claim: miR-142 controls a network of chief actin regulators to facilitate MK terminal differentiation.
source: In summary, our analysis suggests a cardinal role for miR-142 in maturation of MKs, and in particular in controlling a network of chief actin regulators to facilitate MK terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the target validation and rescue experiments.

claim: The data challenges the prevailing paradigm that miRNAs exert only subtle effects, often elicited by specific stressors.
source: The data challenges the prevailing paradigm, that miRNAs exert only subtle effects, often elicited by specific stressors (Ebert and Sharp, 2012; Mendell and Olson, 2012; Pelaez and Carthew, 2012), by providing in vivo evidence that genetic manipulation of a single miRNA may have a significant impact on cellular commitment and differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings with citations to prior views.

claim: Genetic manipulation of a single miRNA may have a significant impact on cellular commitment and differentiation.
source: The data challenges the prevailing paradigm, that miRNAs exert only subtle effects, often elicited by specific stressors (Ebert and Sharp, 2012; Mendell and Olson, 2012; Pelaez and Carthew, 2012), by providing in vivo evidence that genetic manipulation of a single miRNA may have a significant impact on cellular commitment and differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the strong phenotypes observed in miR-142 knockout mice.

claim: Several platelet disorders have been associated with mutations in genes involved in actin organization.
source: Several platelet disorders have been associated with mutations in genes involved in actin organization, including Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) (Massaad et al., 2013) and Actinin alpha 1 (ACTN1) (Kunishima et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: The miR-142 locus is involved in B-cell leukemogenesis.
source: Because miR-142 locus is involved in B-cell leukemogenesis (Gauwerky et al., 1989) and since miR-142 is necessary for CD4+ DCs development (Mildner et al., 2013) and MK differentiation, miR-142 may function as a broad hematopoietic pro-differentiation factor.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: miR-142 may function as a broad hematopoietic pro-differentiation factor.
source: Because miR-142 locus is involved in B-cell leukemogenesis (Gauwerky et al., 1989) and since miR-142 is necessary for CD4+ DCs development (Mildner et al., 2013) and MK differentiation, miR-142 may function as a broad hematopoietic pro-differentiation factor.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the multiple roles of miR-142 in different hematopoietic lineages.

claim: Changes in miR-142 levels or activity may lead to platelet disorders or to hematopoietic malignancies.
source: Thus, changes in miR-142 levels or activity may lead to platelet disorders or to hematopoietic malignancies.
evidence: This is speculation about the clinical implications of the findings.
